part2.intro: Three young people talk about travelling around a city they visited on holiday.
part2.question: For each question, choose the correct answer.

texts.label: A
texts.title: Daniel
texts.text: Last spring I went to Tokyo with my dad. We used the underground every day. The trains were very clean and they were never late – not even one minute! But the map of the underground was really difficult to understand. On our first day we took the wrong train and went to the other side of the city. In the end, a kind passenger showed us the right way.

texts.label: B
texts.title: Sara
texts.text: I visited Venice in Italy with my family last summer. There are no cars in the city at all! Instead of buses, people travel on boats called water buses. They were great fun, but the tickets cost a lot of money, so we walked most of the time. We crossed lots of little bridges over the canals. My feet hurt every evening!

texts.label: C
texts.title: Phong
texts.text: In October I went to London with my school. My favourite thing was travelling on the red buses. They have two floors, and I always ran to get the front seat upstairs because you can see everything from there. We also went on a boat tour along the river. It rained almost every day, but I didn't mind because there were so many things to see.

items.q: Who visited a city with no cars?
Who had a problem finding the right way?
Who liked sitting in one special place?
Who says travelling was very expensive?
Who says the transport was always on time?
Who had bad weather?
Who walked a lot?

part3.title: To Asia without a plane
part3.text:
Most people who travel from Europe to Asia take a plane. The flight takes about twelve hours. But last summer, thirteen-year-old Felix Weber and his mother travelled from Berlin to Hanoi to visit his grandparents – and they didn't get on a plane once. The journey took them nineteen days.

"Mum and I wanted to see the countries between Germany and Vietnam, not just the sky," says Felix. "And planes are bad for the environment." His father couldn't travel with them because he had to work, so he flew out to meet them at the end.

They travelled mostly by train. The longest part of the journey was the train across Russia and Mongolia, which took six days. "I thought I'd be bored, but I wasn't," says Felix. "I played cards with other passengers and watched the view from the window for hours."

There were some problems, too. In China, their train was delayed for nine hours because of a problem with the engine. "We slept on the floor of the station," Felix says. "It wasn't fun, but now it's a funny story."

When they finally arrived in Hanoi, Felix's grandparents met them at the railway station. "My grandma cried when she saw us," he remembers.

Felix wrote a blog during the trip, and lots of people read it. "Next summer, Mum and I want to travel to Spain by bike," he says. "Maybe I'll write a book about that journey!"

items.q: Why did Felix and his mother decide not to fly?
options: They wanted to see more places.

items.q: What do we learn about Felix's father?
options: He went to Vietnam by plane.
He stayed at home with the grandparents.
He drove them to the station in Berlin.

items.q: What does Felix say about the train across Russia?
options: He was bored most of the time.
He found lots of things to do.

items.q: What happened in China?
options: They had to wait a long time.

items.q: What is Felix planning to do next?

part4.title: The first long car journey
part4.text:
In August 1888, a German woman called Bertha Benz {19} history. Her husband, Karl, had built one of the first cars, but he didn't believe it could travel very far. Bertha wanted to show him that he was wrong.

Early one morning, she and her two teenage sons {20} the house without telling Karl. They drove 106 kilometres to visit her mother in another town. There were no petrol stations then, so Bertha had to buy fuel from a chemist's shop {21} the way.

The journey wasn't easy. The car had no roof, and the roads were very bad. When the brakes stopped working, Bertha {22} them herself with help from a shoemaker. The car couldn't go up hills, so the boys had to get out and {23} it.

They arrived in the evening, and Bertha sent a message to Karl. Her journey showed people that cars were useful, and soon many people wanted to {24} one.

part7.instruction: Look at the three pictures. Write the story shown in the pictures. Write 35 words or more.

part7.model: Last Saturday Anna took the tram into the city centre. She put her bag on the seat next to her and looked out of the window. When she got off, she forgot her bag! She ran to the tram station and asked for help. Later, the tram driver gave her the bag. She was so happy.

items.q: What did the boy forget to pack?

script.t: Have you got everything for the trip, Leo? What about your passport?
Yes, it's in my bag with my ticket.
And your sunglasses?
I'm wearing them! Oh no – my phone charger. It's still next to my bed at home.
Don't worry, you can borrow mine.

items.q: How will the family get to the airport?

script.t: Shall we get a taxi to the airport tomorrow?
It's too expensive. What about the bus? It stops right outside our house.
But it takes almost two hours. The train only takes forty minutes.
OK, let's do that. The station isn't far, and we can walk there with our suitcases.

items.q: What time does the flight leave?

script.t: What time's our flight, Dad? Nine fifteen?
No, that's when we have to be at the airport. The flight leaves at ten fifty.
And when do we arrive in Paris?
At about one o'clock, if there aren't any delays.

items.q: What does the woman's son want to be?

script.t: Your son loves planes, doesn't he? Does he want to be a pilot?
He did when he was little. Now he's more interested in how planes work.
So an engineer?
Yes, he wants to design plane engines. His best friend wants to be a train driver, but that's not for him.

items.q: What does the boy's Uncle Mark drive?

script.t: Your Uncle Mark drives a coach, doesn't he? He took us on the school trip.
No, that was my other uncle, Uncle Tony. Uncle Mark drives a lorry.
Oh! Does he go far?
Yes, all over Europe. He was a taxi driver when he was young, but he loves long journeys more.

part2.intro: You will hear a teacher telling students about a visit to an airport.
part2.title: Class Visit to City Airport

script.t: OK, everyone, listen carefully. Our visit to City Airport is next week. It was on Monday, but the airport asked us to change it, so we're going on Tuesday instead. The coach will leave from the school gate at half past eight, so please be there by quarter past. The journey takes about an hour if the traffic isn't bad. When we arrive, we'll watch the planes taking off from the top floor of the airport. After that, we'll go inside a real plane, and you can sit in the seats and look at the engines. A pilot is going to talk to us about his job, so think of some good questions. Last year, students met one of the engineers, but this year he isn't free. For lunch, there's a café at the airport. A sandwich and a drink cost five pounds. Or you can bring your own lunch if you prefer. Our guide at the airport is Mrs Brennan. That's B-R-E-N-N-A-N. And remember – you don't need your passport, because we aren't flying anywhere!

part3.intro: You will hear a girl, Ella, asking a man at a tourist information centre about travelling around a city.

items.q: How long is Ella's family staying in the city?
Where can't they use their travel card?
How will they get to the castle?
Why is the boat tour free for children today?
What does the man say about the railway museum?
options: Visitors can drive a model train there.
It is next to the bridge.

script.t: Hello. I'm here with my family for three days. What's the best way to get around the city?
The trams are the quickest. You can buy a travel card for one day for eight pounds, or for three days for eighteen pounds.
Three days, please. We arrived this morning and we're leaving on Sunday. Can we use the card on the buses too?
Yes, on the buses and the trams, but not on the underground. That's a different ticket.
OK. We'd like to visit the castle tomorrow. How do we get there?
Take tram number four from the stop outside. It's about fifteen minutes. You could walk, but it's a long way, and it's all uphill. There's no bus that goes there.
The tram, then. And is there a boat tour on the river?
Yes, there's one every hour from the bridge. It usually costs ten pounds, but today it's free for children because it's a national holiday.
Brilliant! My little brother loves boats. Is there anything else we should see?
The railway museum is very popular. It's open every day except Monday. There are lots of old trains, and you can even drive a model train.
My dad will love that! Can I take a map, please?
Here you are. It's free, and it shows all the tram stops.

items.intro: You will hear a girl talking to her friend about her first flight.
items.q: How did the girl feel during the flight?

script.t: How was your flight to Spain, Amy? It was your first one, wasn't it?
Yes! I thought I'd be scared, but I wasn't at all.
Long flights can be boring, though.
It was only two hours, and I looked out of the window the whole time. When we went up through the clouds, I couldn't stop smiling!

items.intro: You will hear a man talking about traffic on the radio.
items.q: What is the problem on the motorway?
options: The road is closed for repairs.

script.t: And now the traffic news. There are long delays on the motorway this morning, near the airport. A lorry has stopped on the road with an engine problem, and a mechanic is on the way. There's no accident, and no one is hurt, but drivers should leave home early. And the road repairs on Bridge Street have finished, so that road is open again.

items.intro: You will hear a boy talking about his grandmother.
items.q: What does the boy say about his grandmother?
options: She has visited lots of countries.

script.t: My grandma is seventy-two, but she's always travelling. Last year she went to Peru, and this spring she's going to Japan. She's been to about forty countries now! She doesn't enjoy long flights, but she says it's worth it. She stopped working ten years ago, so now she has lots of time to explore.

items.intro: You will hear a boy talking to his mother at a petrol station.
items.q: Why have they stopped at the petrol station?

script.t: Mum, why are we stopping here? We've got lots of petrol.
I know. But the car felt strange on the motorway, so I want to look at the tyres.
Can I get some crisps from the shop while you do that?
No, we'll have lunch soon. Wait in the car, please.

items.intro: You will hear a girl leaving a message for her mother.
items.q: Why is the girl calling?

script.t: Hi Mum, it's me. I'm at the station. I'm really sorry, but I missed the four o'clock train. The bus from school was slow because of the traffic, and when I got to the platform, the train was just leaving. Don't worry, I've still got my ticket, and I can use it on the next train. It arrives at quarter past five. Can you meet me then?

part5.intro: You will hear Hugo talking to his friend Nadia about a family holiday. What did each person forget to bring?

script.t: Hi Hugo! How was your holiday in Italy?
Good, but my family forgot so many things! Dad forgot his passport. We were already on the motorway, and we had to drive back home to get it.
Oh no! Did you miss the flight?
No, luckily. And Dad had all our tickets on his phone, so that was OK.
And your mum? She's usually so organised.
She packed everything, but she left her sunglasses on the kitchen table. It was really sunny, so she had to buy some at the airport.
What about your sister?
Lily forgot her camera. She was upset, because she wanted to take photos of the beach. She used Mum's phone instead.
Your grandpa came too, didn't he?
Yes. He remembered to bring a map of the city, but he forgot his umbrella. And of course it rained on the second day!
And you? Did you remember everything?
I thought so. But when we opened the suitcases at the hotel, I didn't have my swimming shorts! I had to borrow some from Grandpa. They were enormous!
